appraisal_events.evidence: His nephew's marriage joins up his scattered aristocratic scraps and "Legrandin eut une situation mondaine" retroactively solidified by ladies who now recall twenty years of visits; "Couvert par le duc de Guermantes, Legrandin fut... le véritable comte de Méséglise" — a title the narrator calls false, and the man himself is shown bolting into houses "où il ne faut pas être vu" and disclaiming what everyone says of Charlus.
appraisal_events.explanation: Legrandin's standing rises decisively and durably, but the narration keeps the mechanism visible — retroactive credit, an invented county, and a snobbery that only yields because a coarser vice has replaced it.

appraisal_events.evidence: She believed the name Saint-Loup had become an enamel fixed on her, "ce qui était une erreur, car la valeur d'un titre de noblesse... monte quand on le demande et baisse quand on l'offre"; "le milieu que recevait la marquise dépréciait le nom qu'elle portait", and she ends by declaring the whole Faubourg idiotic and yawning in the face of its most brilliant callers.
appraisal_events.explanation: Having reached the summit she squanders it, and the narrator states as a law that her salon drags her name down — a diminishment the narration itself pronounces rather than merely reports.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Ce jeune homme qui avait paru à une époque si fier, si ambitieux, invitait à partager son luxe des camarades que sa mère n'aurait pas reçus"; "Saint-Loup fort à genoux devant sa femme... parce qu'il lui devait précisément ce luxe extrême"; the receptions of Mme de Marsantes and Mme de Forcheville give way to "un nid silencieux".
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage measures the collapse of his ambition against his mother's and mother-in-law's brilliant salons, and grounds his compliance in the fortune he owes his wife.

appraisal_events.evidence: "La personne qui profita le moins de ces deux unions" died of typhoid weeks after the wedding, yet the faire-part mingles Jupien's name with Montmorency, Bourbon-Soissons, Modène-Este, lady Essex: "la mort de la petite roturière met en deuil toutes les familles princières de l'Europe".
appraisal_events.explanation: The alliance confers on the tailor's niece a princely European standing that arrives only in time for her funeral, an elevation the narration frames as pure mechanism ("le tout, en effet, est d'avoir une grande alliance").

status_effects.explanation: He passes from isolated invitations to a genuine social position, and the duc de Guermantes' cover makes him the comte de Méséglise for a whole generation.
The same paragraphs discredit him: the borrowed title, the hidden haunts, the tennis and cavalry-officer figure kept up to mask his age, the pretended ignorance about Charlus.
Her name loses its purchasing power as she spends it on a milieu that depreciates it, and she ends by receiving no one of the society she had wanted.
He is on his knees before his wife, dependent on her fortune for the ease he now prefers to ambition.
The household that should have inherited two of the most brilliant salons in Paris gives no reception at all, a regression the world is shown remembering.
The faire-part places her among the princely houses of Europe and can pass her off to a new generation as a lady of the highest birth.
